name: Maré
title: Maré: the biggest week of the year
lede: A fashion retailer that sells through a site, an app and 38 stores. Two decisions decide how much it earns on Black Friday: one behind the scenes, one on the screen.

context.label: What it sells
context.text: Fashion in reais, online and in 38 stores, with its own store card and a creator program.

context.label: Why this week
context.text: Black Friday packs a large share of the quarter's sales into a few hours, and the busiest minute is at midnight.

context.label: What already works
context.text: Checkout saves each order once and tells every other part on one feed, so a slow partner fails alone.

problems.label: Backend problem
problems.title: Black Friday without losing a sale
problems.question: How do we protect and grow sales on the busiest night of the year, at a cost we chose on purpose?
bullets: Not every click is worth the same: protect paying first
A fair line beats a crash when checkout is full
Decide in October what switches off in November

problems.label: Frontend problem
problems.title: Live truth on a ready-made storefront
problems.question: How do we keep pages fast and cheap while never showing a price or stock that checkout will reject?
bullets: Keep the fast ready-made pages exactly as they are
Make only price, stock and the bag live
Design the busy version of every page in advance

levels.name: Lean
levels.off: Personal suggestions become this week's bestsellers. Videos stop playing on their own.
levels.trigger: Checkout p95 over target for 2 min, or the extras pool saturated · automatic

levels.name: Focused
levels.off: Search keeps its most used filters. New store-card applications and office exports pause.
levels.trigger: Checkout error budget burning 14.4× · a person approves

levels.name: Line
levels.off: New checkouts wait in a fair line. Every bag stays reserved while its owner waits.
levels.notice: A short line with a wait time
levels.trigger: Checkout concurrency at the load-tested admission limit

levels.name: Checkout only
levels.off: Browsing is served from saved pages. Everything except orders waits for later.
levels.trigger: Orders database or payments in partial failure

backend.decision: Pay for Black Friday readiness, sized by the sales an outage would cost, and agree in advance what switches off first.
backend.alternative: Keep sizing everything for an average day.
backend.why: Sales at five past midnight are worth many ordinary minutes, and the failures that matter (hot deals, payment slowdowns, a flood of connections) only appear at that scale.
changes: Sales per minute at the peak
giveUp: A higher bill for about one week
Suggestions and some filters off at the peak
Some shoppers wait in a line
Weeks of engineering before the event instead of new features
wrong: Too little: the site fails at the most valuable minute of the year, and those sales don't come back.
Too much: money spent on capacity that sits idle. The “is it worth it” math is how to find the middle.

frontend.decision: Keep the storefront ready-made. Make only price, stock, the bag and busy mode live, show stock honestly, and let pages simplify on a plan.
frontend.alternative: Rebuild the storefront to build every page on request.
frontend.why: The most expensive disappointment in retail is finding out at payment that an item is gone. The second is a page that breaks while checkout itself is fine.
changes: Add to bag → paid, at the peak
Cost per visit (more stays on nearby servers)
giveUp: Exact stock counts become simple bands
Extras disappear at the peak, by design
Time spent on simpler twins nobody sees on a good day
wrong: Fully ready-made: we sell sold-out items, cancel orders and pay for it in support and reputation.
Built on every request: our own computers carry all the traffic, the bill rises, and the site is slowest exactly when it matters.

concepts.title: Capacity planning
concepts.line: Concurrency = throughput × time (Little's law): where the first wall is, before a load test finds it.

concepts.title: Admission control
concepts.line: Why waiting time explodes near full use, and why a fair line beats scaling forever.

concepts.title: Hot keys
concepts.line: Locks, sharded counters and why the hardest scaling problem is often one row.

concepts.title: Idempotency
concepts.line: Safe to retry makes every other resilience technique possible.

concepts.title: Outbox and backpressure
concepts.line: A spike becomes a queue that catches up; checkout never waits.

concepts.title: Bulkheads and retry budgets
concepts.line: Stopping one failure from becoming every failure.

concepts.title: Graceful degradation
concepts.line: Decide what to switch off in advance; build the busy version as a real screen.

concepts.title: Cache hierarchies
concepts.line: Ready-made at the edge, a two-second shared answer, and when staleness is a feature.

concepts.title: SLOs in money
concepts.line: Sales per minute, burn rates and error budgets as the language with the business.

concepts.title: Cost as a design input
concepts.line: Expected-loss arithmetic, and paying for the peak only while it happens.

screens.title: Maré: the biggest week of the year

steps.title: One retailer, one week
steps.caption: A fashion retailer in Brazil, and the one week that decides its quarter.
steps.presenterNote: Maré sells fashion online and in 38 stores, and one week decides its quarter. Everything here is fictitious, but the problems are real.

steps.title: Behind the scenes
steps.caption: Protect and grow sales on the busiest night of the year, at a cost we chose.
steps.presenterNote: The first problem is behind the scenes: how do we keep selling at midnight on Black Friday without paying for that capacity all year?

steps.title: On the screen
steps.caption: Keep pages fast and cheap, and never show a price or stock that checkout will reject.
steps.presenterNote: The second is on the screen: the store is fast because it's ready-made, so how do we keep that and still tell the truth about stock?

screens.title: Black Friday without losing a sale
The plan for a bad night

steps.title: Level 1 · Lean
steps.caption: The first thing to go is what shoppers miss least: personal suggestions become bestsellers.
steps.presenterNote: Level one happens on its own. Suggestions become bestsellers and most shoppers never notice.

steps.title: Level 2 · Focused
steps.caption: Search keeps its most used filters, and anything that can wait until Monday waits.
steps.presenterNote: Level two pauses what can wait until Monday, like new store-card applications and office exports.

steps.title: Level 3 · Line
steps.caption: New checkouts wait in a fair line, and every bag stays reserved while its owner waits.
steps.presenterNote: Level three is the waiting line. The promise is simple: your bag is safe while you wait.

steps.title: Level 4 · Checkout only
steps.caption: If something big fails, browsing runs from saved pages and only orders are taken live.
steps.presenterNote: Level four is the last resort: we stop everything except taking orders, and we've rehearsed it.

screens.title: The decision: pay for the peak, on purpose

steps.title: The decision
steps.caption: Pay for readiness, sized by what an outage would cost, and agree in advance what switches off first.
steps.presenterNote: The decision isn't technical: it's whether to pay for the peak, and how much, and what we agree to give up.

steps.title: What changes
steps.caption: Sales per minute at the peak, checkouts that succeed, payments approved, and zero items sold twice.
steps.presenterNote: These are the numbers it moves, and sales per minute at the peak is the one that matters most.

steps.title: Is it worth it?
steps.caption: Compare the sales an outage would likely cost with what readiness costs. Move the sliders.
steps.presenterNote: This is the whole argument in one line: keep spending while every R$1 of readiness removes more than R$1 of expected loss.

steps.title: What we give up
steps.caption: A bigger bill for one week, fewer extras at the peak, and some shoppers in a short line.
steps.presenterNote: And this is the price, said out loud, so nobody is surprised on the night.

screens.title: Live truth on a ready-made storefront
Try it: one deal on Black Friday night

steps.title: Watch the stock
steps.caption: Others are buying. The band changes, the page never jumps, and our systems are asked once every 2 seconds.
steps.presenterNote: Press the button a few times: the stock drops, the band changes, and nothing on the page moves.

steps.title: Add to bag
steps.caption: With plenty left it's instant. With a few left it says reserving and confirms.
steps.presenterNote: Now add it to the bag, first with plenty in stock and then with only a few left.

steps.title: Turn up the pressure
steps.caption: Raise the busy level and watch the page get simpler while the buy button keeps working.
steps.presenterNote: Finally, turn up the pressure: the page gets simpler, and buying still works at every level.

screens.title: The decision: keep what works, make the truth live

steps.title: The decision
steps.caption: Keep the store ready-made, make only the fast-changing parts live, and design the busy version in advance.
steps.presenterNote: The frontend decision is mostly about what we don't do: we don't rebuild a storefront that already works.

steps.title: What changes
steps.caption: More bags become paid orders at the peak, and far fewer shoppers hear “no longer available” at payment.
steps.presenterNote: The numbers it moves are about trust at the moment of paying.

steps.title: What we give up
steps.caption: Exact stock counts, some extras at the peak, and marketing trackers on the checkout page.
steps.presenterNote: And the price is honest too: less precise scarcity, fewer extras at the peak, and less tracking on checkout.

points: Both decisions protect the same number: sales per minute at the peak.
The backend decides what to protect and what to give up; the frontend makes giving up look calm instead of broken.
Atlas and Pulse follow the same pattern: one decision behind the scenes, one on the screen.
